It's more to do with association than logic; up until the 1930s fragrances were unisex, the only things really directed towards men were aftershaves, but much like the Romans' aftershaves, these were primarily for medical purposes, however, after the release of Pour Un Homme which was a wild success with its deep base notes that we would typically perceive to be "masculine" (even if the perfume in its entirety could be considered not very masculine), a slew of companies creating similarly geared, and based, perfumes exploded onto the market, creating the idea of a "masculine scent", and in contrast, a "feminine scent". In the 90s a few "cleaner" scents were introduced, and now some of the smaller companies are bringing back "neutral" scents or doing away with gendering their scents all together.

So if your father wore a "masculine" scent with spicy, woody notes, you're more likely to associate that with the idea of masculinity, and if your mother wore a lighter, floral scent, you're going to associate that with femininity. There's also a cultural element in there as well; different cultures, and indeed different time periods, are going to have different associations with different scents depending on locality and significance of certain flowers, plants, spices etc, so a "masculine" scent in Europe and America may not be seen as one in, say, India.
